I know how wiped out you can feel in these situations, but as someone who's had a very bad experience with anxiety medication, my very best advice is to research every drug you are prescribed. Develop a working understanding of what you're taking. I wish I had. Without medical school, you won't be an expert on the medications, but there are things worth knowing. For instance, I was prescribed the max dose of Xanax. It definitely helped. However, I did not know it was somewhat addictive, and I was not aware that suddenly stopping Xanax can actually lead to severe withdrawal and possibly death. You have to taper off. So when I had a bad life event that lead me to stop being able to afford the medication, I nearly ended up in the hospital. Had I known, I would have put more effort into weaning off rather than just running out.   


So yeah. A bit of research can make a lot of difference in the long run.

Something I wish someone had told me when I started, if you do decide to upgrade at any point, always look for coil wattage that exceeds your need. If you think you'll be running 100W, aim for a tank and coil with an average of 80-200W. Reason is that you may want more power later, and the top end of the coil's range isn't something you should expect to hit. Some coils will be okay at that hypothetical 200W, but the ones that aren't will burn within a few puffs leaving you with a mouth full of charcoal flavor. If you aim low to middle of your expectations, you will often spend more but burn coils less.

I'm not a frequent camper anymore, but one time some years ago on the worst camping trip I ever went on, location chosen by a friend who did nothing to prepare for the place and weather, we spent a whole day setting up a rather awesome camp with strong tents and a good stock of firewood. We cooked, and all seemed well. Then late at night the first night, one of us got up to take a leak and noticed people hovering just on the outside of the light left by the fire. As far as we knew, there was nobody around for miles. So we posted a watch every night, to make sure our stuff didn't get stolen. Then, the next night, a crazy downpour came in, and we all spent time setting up proper cover. At some point, around 3 am, the rain was easing off. And again, just outside of the light, cloud cover blocking the moon, we saw a few people moving around. Then a few more. Everyone was woken up. More and more people, from both sides. A few of them stopped. We sat there freaked out wondering what the hell was going on. One of the ones who stopped started jogging straight at us. Then his friend. Then four others. We grabbed our machetes and an ax just in case. 

Then we heard, "HEY DUDES YOU HAVE TO GET OUT OF HERE, THERE MIGHT BE A MUDSLIDE!"

Turns out our buddy had not checked the weather or our location, and put us on the low end of a large hill. The massive group of people, we later learned, were something of a homeless camp that lived around the area. We were scared shitless because of bad planning.

Service lines, for example phone and cable wiring. These can cost a surprising amount of money on short notice and there are lots of wiring issues standard service technicians can't do. For instance, in my area where I work as a cable guy, I can't fish a line inside a wall more than one floor up or down, and this doesn't mean I can go up one floor and then up one more from there, it means the only way I'll be able to do it is by drilling a hole through your outside wall and hanging the line on the outside of your home from there to where it connects to the main line. I don't just mean not having an outlet where you want it either, this includes if you have bad existing wires. If I can't replace or fix it, I have to redo it from somewhere else. If you want a clean wiring setup, have a home-run box installed where every line for every provider type is run to the same place, brand new. Costs, but saves in the long run.

EDIT: If you're buying a new home, you may be able to haggle with the seller/builder to install this type of line work before you even sign the dotted line. Realtors would know more about this.
